final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral package: 3.5% dairy access over six years with permanent supply-management carve-out, 70-72.5-75% auto phase-in, and binding labor enforcement (on-site inspections, remedies, independent monitors) all locked in treaty text by September 1, targeting October 15 signature. Canada committed conditional on written legal confirmation; USTR and Mexico accepted. However, serious ratification risk emerged as Congress's ability to hold the locked language through November remained unaddressed.
minority_objections: Auto industry and supply-chain manufacturers raised persistent concern that Congressional reopening of labor or Chapter 19 language post-September 1 would unravel supply-chain certainty despite locked treaty text
key_conflicts: Canada initially resisted 3.6% dairy access as politically unsellable; U.S. anchored to Korea precedent
Tension over whether September 1 legal drafting was achievable without slipping October 15 signature deadline
Implicit conflict between locking treaty text early (September 1) versus maintaining Congressional flexibility for November ratification
key_concessions: U.S. moved from 3.6% to 3.5% dairy access and accepted six-year phase-in
U.S. accepted permanent Chapter 19 carve-out for Canadian supply management
U.S. accepted auto phase-in (70-72.5-75%) instead of immediate 75% floor
Mexico agreed to add independent union monitors to inspection protocol for trilateral package
Canada accepted 3.5% dairy access and committed to October 15 signature conditional on written legal confirmation
red_lines: Canada: supply management disputes permanently carved out of Chapter 19 (stated multiple times as 'non-negotiable')
U.S.: labor enforcement must include on-site inspections with binding remedies in treaty text (Congress ratification requirement)
U.S.: September 1 legal drafting deadline non-negotiable to hit October 15 signature and November Congressional vote
USTR: if Canada reopens dairy or Chapter 19 after September 1, U.S. proceeds bilaterally with Mexico
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Congressional capacity to reopen or amend locked treaty language during November ratification process (raised by auto industry, labor union, supply-chain manufacturers but never answered by USTR or Congress)
Feasibility of legal team actually completing both labor and auto drafting by September 1 (questioned repeatedly but only met with assurances, no process detail)
Political risk in Canada if October 15 signature slips and producers lose confidence (mentioned by Canada but not addressed with contingency)
downstream_risk_variables: Whether USTR legal team actually delivers binding treaty text by September 1
Whether Congress attempts to amend labor enforcement or Chapter 19 language during November ratification despite September 1 lock
Whether Canada's government can sell 3.5% dairy access domestically once treaty text is public
Whether supply chains commit reshoring investment before or after November ratification vote
uncertainty_notes: USTR's mechanism to prevent Congressional reopening of locked language remained unspecified. Legal team's capacity to draft both labor and auto chapters by September 1 was asserted but not demonstrated. Canada's final commitment was conditional on written confirmation not yet provided in the meeting. Sunset clause was mentioned once by Congress but never discussed.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: Auto phase-in (70-72.5-75%) was negotiated as a core concession to unlock Canada's participation; supply-chain manufacturers made reshoring investment conditional on locked auto numbers; drove the September 1 legal drafting ultimatum.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Labor enforcement (on-site inspections, binding remedies, independent monitors) was stated by Congress as a ratification requirement; drove USTR's September 1 legal drafting deadline and Mexico's agreement to add union monitors; shaped the entire package timeline.
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy access was the primary U.S.-Canada negotiation point; moved from 3.6% to 3.5% as the compromise that unlocked Canada's October 15 commitment; permanent Chapter 19 carve-out was Canada's condition for signing.
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Chapter 19 carve-out for supply management was stated as 'non-negotiable' and 'permanent' by Canada multiple times, and U.S./Mexico accepted it as part of the package, but it did not block progress—it was accommodated rather than fought over.
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Sunset clause mentioned once by Congress in passing ('sunset clause, Chapter 19 scope') but never discussed, debated, or shaped any proposal.
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congressional ratification risk drove the September 1 legal drafting deadline, the October 15 signature target, and the November vote window; multiple actors (auto industry, labor, supply-chain) raised concern that Congressional reopening of locked text would unravel the deal; shaped USTR's ultimatum strategy.
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Supply-chain manufacturers raised compliance cost and sourcing adjustment concerns repeatedly (reshoring capital, supplier reorganization conditional on locked treaty text), but these were acknowledged and addressed via the auto phase-in—did not change the room's direction, only reinforced the September 1 deadline.
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: USTR explicitly used the U.S.-Mexico bilateral as leverage ('we move forward without you'; 'you're left holding the bag'); Mexico joined this pressure ('what else do you need, or are we signing?'); this was the primary mechanism forcing Canada to accept 3.5% dairy and commit to October 15.

node: Node 1 - North American Trade Negotiation Room (after the 27 Aug 2018 U.S.-Mexico preliminary agreement, before the final trilateral USMCA package; information cutoff 2018-08-27)
